title: Competition in Generative AI: Evidence from Consumer Demand
content:
Competition in Generative AI: Evidence from Consumer Demand
How competitive will the market for generative AI be as it matures? Using novel transaction level credit and debit card data covering 174 million consumers and 114 billion transactions, we study the adoption of paid services and the demand-side foundations of competition in this market. As of April 2026, approximately 2.9% of U.S. consumers pay for at least one major generative AI service, with adoption highest among younger and higher-income consumers. Nearly all of these paid users subscribe to basic plans that cost $30 or less per month. Three patterns suggest limited differentiation and low switching costs. First, although multihoming is common, it has declined as providers’ capabilities have expanded. Second, annual customer retention rates range from 20% to 45% across major AI providers, lower than those for many other subscription products. Third, switching rises around major model releases. Motivated by these findings, we develop and estimate a structural model of AI service demand and supply that reveals strong competitive pressure. Consumers are highly price sensitive, have much weaker preferences for particular providers than for AI overall, and view AI services as increasingly close substitutes. Our results suggest that, absent a substantial increase in AI model quality differentiation, growing substitutability among services will constrain providers’ pricing power and allow consumers to capture a large share of the surplus generated by these services.

report.summary: Card-transaction data show U.S. generative AI subscriptions are low-margin and highly substitutable, with weak retention and strong price competition limiting providers' pricing power.
report.background: Generative AI providers have spent heavily on models and compute, betting that consumer subscriptions will become durable, high-margin revenue. Early pricing settled around $20–$30 per month, with providers arguing that capability leadership, memory, and ecosystem lock-in would create moats. This NBER paper tests that assumption using transaction-level credit and debit card data covering 174 million U.S. consumers and 114 billion transactions. It measures who pays for AI, how many services they buy, how long they stay, and how demand responds to new model releases. The results arrive as the industry faces rising capex and questions about whether consumer AI is a commodity business or a differentiated platform market.
key_points: Paid adoption is still narrow. As of April 2026, only about 2.9% of U.S. consumers pay for at least one major generative AI service. Users skew younger and higher-income, and almost all pay for basic tiers costing $30 or less per month. That leaves a large non-paying base and suggests monetization is still early.

Multihoming is common but falling. Many paying users subscribe to more than one AI service, but this behavior has declined as providers' capabilities expanded. Consumers appear to consolidate around fewer tools rather than spreading spend, a pattern consistent with services becoming closer substitutes rather than more differentiated.

Retention is weak. Annual customer retention rates range from 20% to 45% across major AI providers, below many other subscription products. Churn spikes around major model releases, indicating that users readily switch to whichever provider currently offers the best capability or price.

Demand is price-sensitive and provider-agnostic. The structural model finds consumers care much more about AI overall than about any particular brand. They are highly price sensitive and treat services as increasingly close substitutes. Strong competitive pressure limits providers' ability to raise prices without losing users.

Consumer surplus is likely to grow. Absent a substantial increase in model-quality differentiation, growing substitutability will constrain pricing power. Providers may struggle to convert capability leadership into durable consumer rents, while users capture a large share of the surplus through lower prices, free tiers, and frequent switching.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the findings challenge the assumption that consumer subscriptions will become high-margin annuities funding massive compute capex. If consumers treat models as interchangeable, providers must differentiate through agents, memory, integrations, enterprise trust, or bundling—not raw model quality alone. For developers, low switching costs and price-sensitive demand favor multi-model routing, abstraction layers, and cost-efficient open-weight models; API prices should stay under pressure. Wrapper apps may benefit from easy acquisition but face churn. For regular users, competition means cheaper plans, generous free tiers, and rapid access to new capabilities, though market consolidation or ad-supported tiers could eventually reduce choice. Regulators may also scrutinize bundling and default placements.
report.tools: OpenRouter for comparing and routing across models, LiteLLM for self-hosted model switching and cost tracking, Ollama or vLLM for testing open-weight alternatives, and Similarweb or Sensor Tower for tracking consumer app adoption. The NBER paper and its data appendices are the best starting point for methodology.
